title: Captions Covered by Buttons? Fix Text Placement in Reels, TikTok and Shorts
description: Diagnose captions hidden by app controls, test long subtitle blocks, and improve placement in Reels, TikTok and Shorts.
body:
If subtitles look correct in your editor but disappear behind buttons after uploading, first check whether the problem is interface overlap or cropping. Interface overlap hides part of the picture beneath controls. Cropping removes part of the picture. Moving your caption can solve the first problem; the second may require changing your framing too.

This guide covers text you add to your video. Platform-generated captions are a separate layer and may behave differently.

Identify which layer is causing the problem

Open the exported file outside the social app and pause at the affected line. If the full caption is already missing, return to the editing project. Check the text box, animation and export frame. A social safe-zone template will not repair text that was cut off during export.

If the exported caption is intact, compare the same moment inside the destination app. Note what covers it: the action buttons, account information, post description or another caption layer. Record the platform and viewing surface instead of assuming every viewer sees the same layout.

YouTube says automatic captions can contain transcription errors and should be reviewed. Fixing placement alone does not fix incorrect wording. YouTube automatic-caption guidance.

Test the widest and tallest caption blocks

Choose three moments: your longest line, your tallest wrapped caption and a line displayed during a busy shot. Short opening captions can pass while later lines reach into the right-side controls.

Open the comparison checker with your exported video. Pause at each moment and draw a manual region around the entire caption block, including its background. These regions are markers you position yourself; the checker does not automatically detect or track your subtitles.

Use the platform interface previews as planning aids. Review the current margins and adjust them when your own in-app preview shows different coverage. A passing result means your marked region clears the selected boundaries, not that every app layout has been tested.

Make the smallest useful edit

Move a caption away from the obstruction before shrinking it. If the right-hand controls cover the end of a line, narrow the text block or rebreak the sentence. If the bottom metadata covers the second line, raise the whole block and check that it does not obscure a face or demonstration.

For example, suppose your marked caption ends at Y:1514 and your chosen planning boundary ends at Y:1500. That is 14 pixels of overlap in that scenario. Moving it upward by 38 pixels leaves 24 pixels of clearance. Those numbers illustrate the calculation; they are not a platform specification.

Apply the change in your editor. Moving a marker in the checker does not move the caption inside your video. Export a new file and repeat the check.

Check readability while the video moves

A caption can fit inside the boundary and still be difficult to read. Play the whole sentence at normal speed on a phone-sized display. Check the background behind every word, not just the paused frame. Try a solid or partly opaque caption background when bright footage defeats the lettering.

Avoid crowding the same space with a hook, subtitles and a call to action. Show secondary messages at a different moment where possible. Keep the spoken message understandable with sound muted, and review names, numbers and punctuation manually.

Before you publish

  • Confirm that the final exported file contains the revised captions.
  • Check the longest caption and every change in caption position.
  • Preview each destination separately, including any additional caption layer.
  • Keep an editable master so a platform-specific version is easy to make.

For a worked example, use the comparison tutorial. The measurement methodology explains why planning margins cannot guarantee identical results across devices.

title: Reel Cover Text Cut Off? Check the Crop Before Redesigning
description: Separate cover cropping from video overlays, test crop scenarios and keep your Reel cover headline readable at thumbnail size.
body:
A cover can look balanced at full size and lose its headline when shown as a smaller tile. Start by separating the cover image from the playing video. A crop preview answers which part of an image remains visible; a video safe-zone preview answers where interface elements may cover that image. You may need both checks.

Do not rebuild your cover around an unexplained pixel template. Establish which surface is failing and test a crop that matches what you actually see.

Compare the original with the affected preview

Save your original cover and inspect it outside Instagram. Then compare it with the cover-selection preview and the affected surface in your account. Note whether the top, bottom or sides are missing, whether the image is repositioned, and whether the text is merely too small to read.

If the whole headline is visible but unreadable at tile size, cropping is not the main problem. Shorten the headline, simplify its background and enlarge the lettering. If part of a letter is missing, investigate the crop and placement first.

Account interfaces and viewing surfaces can differ. The scenarios below are geometry exercises, not claims that Instagram universally uses a particular crop today.

Understand what a centered crop removes

Take a 1080 × 1920 image and keep its full width. A centered 4:5 crop has a height of 1350 pixels, so it removes 285 pixels from the top and 285 from the bottom. A centered 3:4 crop has a height of 1440 pixels, removing 240 pixels at each end. A centered square retains 1080 pixels of height and removes 420 pixels at each end.

These calculations assume a centered crop with no additional zoom. Repositioning changes which edges lose content. They explain why text close to the top of a tall image can disappear in a shorter preview without the original image being damaged.

In the crop previewer, use the available labelled scenario as a stress test. If it differs from your current Instagram preview, treat the in-app result as the relevant evidence and adjust the design accordingly. The tool does not reproduce every account's cover controls.

Build the cover around the message

Put the essential headline and the identifying part of the subject near the center. Let decorative shapes and background detail extend toward the edges. Avoid making a border or line of text depend on a precise edge surviving.

Try a short headline such as “Three Lighting Fixes” instead of a sentence describing the entire video. That is an editorial choice, not an Instagram character limit. At tile size, check whether someone can identify the subject and read the headline without opening the image.

Save a separate cover version rather than editing the only copy. Compare the original and revised images in the same preview so you can tell whether your changes helped.

Recheck the video separately

A cover that survives a crop does not prove that subtitles in the video clear interface controls. Open the playing video in the Reels checker and inspect the hook, subtitles and final call to action. Keep cover checks and playback checks as separate steps in your publishing checklist.

If the preview still looks different

Verify that the intended cover file was selected and that you are comparing the same viewing surface. Keep a screenshot of the preview and record the date and device. Avoid repeatedly resizing from memory: the comparison should identify exactly what moved or disappeared.

CreatorSafeZone distinguishes mathematical crop scenarios from measured platform behavior. Read the evidence methodology before treating any template as a universal Instagram specification.

title: How to Create a Custom Safe-Zone Overlay for Reels, TikTok and Shorts
description: Create a reusable safe-zone overlay with a worked margin example, free transparent PNG and SVG downloads, and a practical Canva workflow.
body:
A safe-zone overlay is a temporary reference layer that helps you position text and logos while designing. It should match your video canvas, sit above your content during review and be removed before the final export.

Canva's ordinary margin guides are not a map of TikTok, Reels or Shorts controls. Canva describes margins and bleed primarily in its layout and print guidance, and documents rulers and guides separately. Canva's guide to margins and rulers.

Download the worked-example overlay

Download the transparent PNG overlay or open the editable SVG source. Both use a 1080 × 1920 canvas with illustrative margins: top 180, right 180, bottom 360 and left 120 pixels. The clear working area is 780 × 1380 pixels, starting at X:120, Y:180.

These are teaching values, not measured or official platform boundaries. Red bands mark the example exclusions; the middle is transparent so your video can show through. Choose margins for your actual destination and preview. You may reuse and modify these original CreatorSafeZone guide files for personal or commercial editing.

Choose the canvas and planning margins

Check the width and height of the design before importing a guide. A 1080 × 1920 guide has a 9:16 aspect ratio. A 720 × 1280 canvas has the same ratio, so uniform scaling can preserve the guide's proportions. A square canvas does not: stretching the guide to fit would change the relationship between its margins and the picture.

Use the guide for the actual delivery frame. If you are also creating a square or landscape version, treat that as another layout to review rather than stretching the vertical layout into shape.

Write down the four margins before drawing. For any canvas, working width equals canvas width minus left and right margins; working height equals canvas height minus top and bottom margins. For our example: 1080 − 120 − 180 = 780, and 1920 − 180 − 360 = 1380. If either result is zero or negative, reduce the margins or choose another canvas.

For ads, start with the reference for that specific ad format. For organic video, compare against the destination app's preview and label your template as a planning reference. Do not combine crop boundaries and interface coverage without explaining which each band represents.

Create the overlay in Canva

Create a blank 1080 × 1920 design. Add four rectangles as guide bands, using these example positions measured from the top-left corner:

  • Top: X:0, Y:0, width 1080, height 180.
  • Bottom: X:0, Y:1560, width 1080, height 360.
  • Left: X:0, Y:180, width 120, height 1380.
  • Right: X:900, Y:180, width 180, height 1380.

The side bands stop at the top and bottom bands so their corners do not stack and become darker. Use a visible red fill with partial transparency. Leave the center empty; do not place a white rectangle over it. Put any labels inside the excluded bands so they do not obstruct the content you are checking.

Use your editor's available size and position controls to align the shapes. Canva documents desktop rulers and guides; availability and menu placement can vary. If precise positioning is difficult on your device, import our ready-made PNG instead of estimating the rectangle sizes by eye.

Save an editable copy, then choose PNG and the transparent-background export option if your Canva plan offers it. Canva lists transparent design downloads as a plan-dependent feature; the ready-made PNG above avoids needing that export feature just to obtain this example. Canva transparent-image information.

Check the downloaded image over a colored background. The middle should reveal the color underneath. A white middle means the export contains an opaque background; a JPG cannot preserve this transparency. Do not use a screenshot as a substitute for a transparent PNG.

Add the guide as a temporary layer

From the comparison checker, choose the appropriate guide export for your workflow. Keep a note of its dimensions, platform or scenario, and selected margins. The exported guide reflects those settings; it is not an official platform approval.

Upload the guide image to your Canva design and position it over the full canvas. This is a manual transfer of an image file, not a connection that synchronizes the checker and Canva. Arrange the layer above the content you are checking. If your editor offers layer locking, lock it after alignment so you do not move it while adjusting text.

Before judging your captions, inspect the guide's alignment at all four edges. A guide that is offset, stretched or cropped can give misleading results even when its shaded regions look plausible.

Position the complete text block

Keep the entire block inside your chosen working area, including its background shape and the ends of long lines. Leave some visual space from the boundary rather than aligning letters directly against it.

If moving the block covers your subject, shorten the message or change when it appears. Reducing every caption to tiny text can solve an overlap problem while creating a readability problem. Review the design at phone size after any substantial edit.

For a video with several scenes, inspect each scene and the longest caption. One carefully aligned opening frame says little about text that appears later. Repeat the review for each destination when their planning boundaries differ.

Remove the guide and verify the export

Keep an editable copy containing the guide, then remove the reference layer from the version you intend to publish. Export the video and open the resulting file outside Canva. Look for leftover colored bands, border lines and labels, including at the end of the timeline.

Load the exported file back into the checker. This confirms you are reviewing the delivered picture rather than an earlier design state. Then inspect the destination app's own preview for account-specific controls and layout differences.

Common problems

  • The overlay does not reach every edge: verify the canvas ratio and image sizing before changing the margins.
  • The text clears the overlay but is unreadable: review size, contrast, line breaks and on-screen duration.
  • The export contains the overlay: remove the reference layer from the publishing copy and export again.
  • The app still covers a label: revise the planning boundaries using the actual preview, then adjust the design.

Optional: adapt the SVG in an HTML page

For a code-based workflow, use the downloadable SVG as an image over a video inside a shared 9:16 container. Give the image and video the same displayed bounds; keep the overlay from receiving pointer input so playback remains usable. Resizing only the video or using a different crop mode will misalign the guide.

The SVG source lists the rectangle coordinates from the worked example, so a developer can edit those numbers for another scenario. Embedding the SVG in HTML displays the guide; it does not automatically bake it into a video or create a Canva template. Use the PNG for the simplest Canva import, and remove all guide layers from the final creative.

For the next review step, follow the comparison-page tutorial.

title: Can You Use an Organic Video Safe-Zone Template for Ads?
description: Choose the right ad safe-zone reference and review final captions and calls to action before handing off your video creative.
body:
Use an organic-video template as an early composition check, but verify an advertisement against its actual format and preview before delivery. An ad can introduce a call to action or other elements that your organic preview did not include. A familiar canvas size does not establish the usable area around those elements.

TikTok's in-feed ad documentation says the safe zone depends on dimensions, caption length and additional formats. It also provides different safe-zone files for ads using anchors. TikTok in-feed ad specifications.

Google likewise explains that overlays, calls to action and buttons can appear in different places depending on the ad format, campaign type and screen. Its video-ad specifications include reference templates. Google video-ad specifications.

Identify the placement before editing

Write down the destination platform, selected ad format, canvas ratio, caption copy and planned call to action. If a colleague is setting up the campaign, ask for those details before you finalize text placement. “A vertical ad” is not enough information to choose a definitive overlay.

Download the current template from the relevant platform documentation when one is available. Keep the source link and access date with the project. Do not reuse a file merely because its filename contains the platform name; it may belong to a different format or older workflow.

Review the parts that must remain visible

Mark the product name, offer, logo and essential explanatory text. For each, ask whether an interface element can cover it and whether it stays readable against the moving background. If your design contains important qualifying information, include that in the layout review rather than treating it as expendable small text.

The vertical ad planning tool can help you explore an editable scenario. Its planning boundaries are not a replacement for campaign-specific requirements or a guarantee of platform approval. Set the boundaries to match your evidence and inspect the entire clip.

Compare the final copy and call to action

Test with the caption and call to action you intend to use. A layout checked with placeholder copy may behave differently when the real text is inserted. Keep enough room around the offer that an interface change does not immediately collide with it.

For example, an organic version might place its final instruction near the bottom. In the ad version, that instruction could compete with the platform's own call-to-action area. Move the instruction, change its timing or simplify the frame, then preview again. This is a design scenario, not a measured universal ad margin.

Use the campaign preview

Google documents a preview gallery and a YouTube preview option for supported Shorts video campaigns. Use the available preview for the campaign you are actually preparing. Google's Shorts preview instructions.

Check every placement included in your delivery plan. If one layout cannot serve them all, create separate versions with clear filenames. Keep the original editable project so the change is deliberate and repeatable.

Handoff checklist

  • Record the intended format and the official reference used.
  • Check the final caption, call to action and any additional format elements.
  • Remove editing overlays before exporting.
  • Review the exported file and campaign preview.
  • Record unresolved differences instead of labelling an untested layout “approved.”

Safe placement is one part of ad preparation. It does not establish policy compliance, correct targeting or campaign performance. This guide addresses layout review only.

title: Black Bars or Cropped Faces in Vertical Video? Check Fit, Fill and Export Size
description: Find the cause of black bars and cropped faces by checking source footage, fit or fill scaling, canvas size and the exported file.
body:
When a vertical export has black bars or cuts off a face, compare three things: the source footage, the editing canvas and the exported file. They can have different dimensions. Selecting a vertical export preset does not necessarily repair a composition built for another frame.

Start with a short duplicate project so you can test changes without damaging your original edit.

Find where the mismatch starts

Open the exported file in a regular video player and inspect its dimensions. If the file is landscape when you intended portrait, review the sequence and export settings. If the file is portrait but the picture occupies only a small area inside it, inspect how the source clip is scaled on the canvas.

Adobe's documentation shows that a sequence's horizontal and vertical frame dimensions determine its aspect ratio. Its separate image-sizing guidance describes scaling imported images to the sequence. These are different controls: the frame and the content inside it both matter. Sequence aspect ratio, imported-image sizing.

Also check whether the bars are already part of the source file. Scaling a picture that contains baked-in bars enlarges those bars too. Return to a clean source if you have one.

Choose what you want to preserve

Fit keeps the whole source picture inside the destination frame. When their ratios differ, space remains around it. You can use a deliberate background instead of leaving that space black.

Fill covers the destination frame while preserving the picture's proportions. Parts of the source extend beyond the edges and are cropped. This can work for a centered subject but can cut off a second speaker or a demonstration near the edge.

Stretching width and height independently avoids empty space by distorting the picture. Check faces, circles and product proportions before accepting a stretched result.

A landscape-to-portrait example

Suppose a 1920 × 1080 landscape clip is fitted into a 1080 × 1920 portrait canvas. Scaling the clip to the canvas width gives a picture about 608 pixels tall. The remaining height needs a background or another intentional layout.

Filling the same portrait canvas scales the source to 1920 pixels tall, making it about 3413 pixels wide. Only 1080 pixels of that width remain visible. This explains why a fill operation can remove much of a landscape shot even though the output dimensions are correct.

These are geometric examples, not recommended crop coordinates. Choose the visible area around the content the viewer needs to understand.

Follow the subject through the whole clip

A crop that works at the opening may fail when someone moves sideways. Scrub through the timeline, especially cuts, gestures and demonstrations. Reposition the crop over time where your editor supports it, or use a fit layout when the full scene matters.

Check captions after reframing. Text baked into the source may be cropped along with the picture; editable text can be repositioned separately. If a subtitle disappears, determine which type you have before attempting a fix.

Verify the actual export

Export a short section containing the hardest shot. Confirm its dimensions and inspect it outside the editor. Once the framing is correct, load the final file into the comparison checker to review interface overlap separately.

CreatorSafeZone previews your media and planning regions; it does not reframe or re-export your video. Make the actual crop and scale changes in your editing project. Finish with each destination's preview, because a correctly framed file can still place text under app controls.
